input: This capital appraisal considers a proposed solar array and brings together the key financial figures that are relevant to the investment decision. The installed cost of the solar array is $1100k, while the expected net saving is $159k per year for 8 years. Using a discount rate of 10%, the present value of the savings is calculated as $848k, which leads to a net present value of $-252k. Taken together, these figures indicate that, on the basis of the estimates used in the appraisal, the present value of the expected savings does not fully cover the installed cost over the period considered. It is also important to note that the savings are based on vendor and utility estimates, and that no saving has yet been measured on a comparable installation. Overall, the appraisal therefore rests on projected savings rather than on measured performance from an installation of this kind, and this point should be kept in mind when the figures are considered. The negative outcome is therefore not a marginal feature of the presentation but a central result of the appraisal as it stands. Even before any question is raised about the reliability of the savings estimates, the discounted value of those savings is already lower than the amount that would need to be committed at the outset, and the evidential position adds a further reason for caution because the savings themselves remain unmeasured.
target: On the stated estimates, the solar array should not proceed: its net present value is $-252k. The installed cost is $1100k and the expected net saving is $159k per year for 8 years. At a discount rate of 10%, the present value of the savings is $848k, which falls short of the installed cost. The shortfall is the decision figure: discounted savings do not repay the capital outlay within the appraisal. The savings are vendor and utility estimates. No saving has yet been measured on a comparable installation, so the appraisal carries estimate risk on its central input. A measured saving from a comparable installation would change the quality of the evidence, though not the arithmetic on the present figures. Until such a measurement exists, the case rests on projected performance, and the negative net present value stands as the appraisal result. The appraisal separates into two questions. The first is arithmetic: on the stated cost, saving, life and discount rate, the project returns less in present-value terms than it costs. The second is evidential: the saving is the figure with no measured installation behind it, so it is also the figure most exposed to revision. Both questions point the same way on the current record. The arithmetic gives a negative result even when the estimates are taken at face value, and the evidence base gives no measured performance with which to argue that the estimates are conservative.
